contradictions.question: Is it always wrong to steal?
contradictions.summary: The Decalogue and its echoes across the Torah, Gospels, and Epistles absolutize the prohibition on stealing, yet Genesis 31:19 reports without condemnation that Rachel stole her father's household gods on her way out of Laban's territory. The law says never; the narrative says sometimes you get away with it.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is predictable — Archer and Kaiser will tell you Rachel's theft isn't approved, it's merely reported, and that descriptive passages don't overturn prescriptive ones. Fine, that's a real distinction. But the narrator of Genesis 31 never censures Rachel, never has Yahweh punish her, and in fact lets her clever deception (sitting on the teraphim while menstruating) carry the scene as a kind of trickster victory. That's not neutral reportage. The Jacob cycle is saturated with sanctioned trickery — Jacob stealing Esau's blessing, Jacob outmaneuvering Laban's flocks — and the text treats these episodes as covenant-aligned rather than covenant-violating. Friedman and Alter both read the ancestral narratives as working from a different moral grammar than the Sinai code: the patriarchs are shrewd operators whose victories get ratified by Yahweh regardless of the means. Layer Exodus 1 on top — the Hebrew midwives lie to Pharaoh and God "deals well with them" — and you have a Hebrew Bible that treats absolute moral commands and narrative ethics as running on different tracks. The contradiction isn't that someone broke a rule; it's that the text doesn't seem to notice a rule was broken.
contradictions.scholarship: Robert Alter, *The Art of Biblical Narrative* (Basic Books, 1981). Richard Elliott Friedman, *Commentary on the Torah* (HarperOne, 2001). Nahum Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary on Gen 31:19-35 (Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982). Walter Brueggemann, *Genesis* (Interpretation; John Knox, 1982).

contradictions.question: Who did Jacob wrestle with?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 32 has Jacob wrestling "a man" at the Jabbok, after which Jacob insists he has "seen God face to face" and names the place Peniel. Hosea 12:4 reaches back to the same episode and calls the opponent an angel. Man, God, or angel — the tradition couldn't make up its mind.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization is that "angel of Yahweh" functions as a circumlocution for God himself, so "angel" and "God" are two names for one encounter. Walton and Hamilton both push this line. It's not crazy — angelophanies and theophanies do blur in the Hebrew Bible. But the tradition history here is messier than the harmonization admits. Benjamin Sommer has mapped the mal'akh YHWH across the Hebrew Bible and argued it reflects a "fluidity model" in which the angel is a small-scale embodiment of Yahweh himself — which salvages the harmonization at one level but concedes the text is operating with a notion of divine multiplicity that later monotheism had to work hard to domesticate. Hosea 12 shows that domestication already underway: the Jabbok story in its Genesis form has Jacob grappling with a divine being close enough to touch and strong enough to dislocate his hip, and Jacob names the place "face of God." By Hosea's time the opponent is named an angel. Friedman reads Genesis 32 as J material preserving an older, more physical conception of the deity that Hosea's Ephraimite tradition was actively reworking. The contradiction isn't a narrator slipping up — it's a fossil record of Israel's evolving discomfort with a God who could lose a wrestling match until sunrise.
contradictions.scholarship: Benjamin D. Sommer, *The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel* (Cambridge, 2009). Richard Elliott Friedman, *Who Wrote the Bible?* (Summit, 1987). Victor P. Hamilton, NICOT on Gen 32:22-32 (Eerdmans, 1995). John H. Walton, NIVAC Genesis (Zondervan, 2001).

contradictions.question: When did Jacob rename Luz to Bethel?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 28 has Jacob naming Luz "Bethel" on his way out of Canaan, before he ever meets Rachel. Genesis 35 has God telling him to rename the same place Bethel after he's come back from Paddan-Aram with a full household — "And Jacob called the name of the place where God spake with him, Bethel." Same town, same name, two different founding moments.
contradictions.commentary: The traditional fix, pressed by Kidner and Mathews, is that Genesis 35 is a re-dedication rather than an original naming — Jacob is simply ratifying the name he already gave the place in chapter 28. The text strains against that reading. Genesis 35:15 uses the same naming formula ("wa-yiqra" plus the place name) that Genesis 28:19 used, with no hint that this is a commemoration of a previous act. The Documentary Hypothesis explanation is cleaner: Friedman, Baden, and Carr all assign Genesis 28 and Genesis 35 to different source strands (typically E in 28, with 35 showing Elohist and Priestly material layered together), each of which preserved an independent tradition about how Bethel got its name. The redactor who stitched Genesis together didn't bother reconciling them because the cult site at Bethel was foundational to both traditions and each source claimed the etiology. This is the same pattern you see with the double naming of Israel (Gen 32 vs. Gen 35), the double covenant with Abraham, and the double promise to Hagar. The contradiction isn't that Jacob forgot he already named it — it's that two separate storytellers each gave Bethel its origin story, and both made it into the final text.
contradictions.scholarship: Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale, 2012). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). David M. Carr, *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* (Westminster John Knox, 1996). Kenneth A. Mathews, NAC on Gen 35:1-15 (B&H, 2005). Derek Kidner, *Genesis* (TOTC; IVP, 1967).

contradictions.question: Who was Bashemath's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 26:34 names Esau's wife Bashemath as the daughter of Elon the Hittite. Genesis 36:2-3 names Esau's wife Bashemath as the daughter of Ishmael. Same Esau, same wife-name, two incompatible fathers-in-law.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist workaround — Archer runs it, so does Kaiser — is that Esau had multiple wives and Bashemath was simply a common name, so Genesis 26 and Genesis 36 are talking about two different women who happened to share it. The problem is that Genesis 36:3 also lists "Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite" as Esau's wife, whereas Genesis 26:34 named that same daughter-of-Elon as Bashemath. The names have been swapped between the two passages, not just duplicated. Sarna and Westermann both treat this as a clear case of conflicting wife-lists preserved in different ancestral traditions. The Priestly genealogist in Genesis 36 was working from a different source than the J/E material in Genesis 26, and the editor who combined them didn't iron out the names. Friedman's source-critical breakdown shows Genesis 36 as largely Priestly toledot material organizing Edomite lineage for a post-exilic audience, whereas Genesis 26:34 sits in an older narrative stratum. Trying to rescue both lists as historically accurate requires positing that Esau had a confusingly redundant naming practice where wives got renamed every few chapters. That's not harmonization — that's damage control.
contradictions.scholarship: Claus Westermann, *Genesis 12-36* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1985). Nahum Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary on Gen 26:34 and 36:2-3 (Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: Who was Anah?
contradictions.summary: Three statements inside Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles can't all be true of the same person: Anah is Zibeon's daughter (Gen 36:2, 14), Anah is Seir's son and Zibeon's brother (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38), and Anah is Zibeon's son (Gen 36:24; 1 Chr 1:40). The Edomite genealogy preserves three mutually exclusive identities for Anah.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonizing tradition — Keil and Delitzsch, later picked up by Archer — runs a "two-Anahs" play: there's Anah-the-Hivite-woman (Esau's mother-in-law) and Anah-the-Horite-man (Seir's son), and the repetition is just the genealogist tracking different people with the same name. Fine as far as it goes, but it doesn't resolve the Genesis 36:24 problem, where Anah is "son of Zibeon" and Zibeon is the one who found hot springs — and that's immediately adjacent to Gen 36:20, where the same Anah is Zibeon's brother. Westermann and Sarna both treat Genesis 36 as a patchwork of Edomite king lists and clan genealogies assembled from multiple sources, each using "Anah" slightly differently. The Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch both try to smooth Genesis 36:2 by reading "son of Zibeon" instead of "daughter," which is exactly what a scribe would do if the contradiction was already showing in the received text. Textual critics like Tov treat this as evidence of early scribal discomfort with the passage. The apologist position requires you to assume a genealogist who repeatedly reused the same name in the same chapter without clarifying which Anah he meant. The critical reading is simpler: the compiler had incompatible source traditions and preserved them all.
contradictions.scholarship: Claus Westermann, *Genesis 12-36* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1985). Nahum Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary on Gen 36 (Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Emanuel Tov, *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: Who was Korah's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 36:5, 14, and 18 all make Korah a son of Esau by Aholibamah. Genesis 36:15-16 just a few verses later lists Korah as one of the clan-chiefs ("dukes") descended from Eliphaz, who was Esau's firstborn — making Korah Esau's grandson, not son.
contradictions.commentary: The favorite apologist escape here — run by Archer and by various evangelical study Bibles — is that there are simply two different Korahs, one an Esau-son and one an Eliphaz-son, and the genealogist just tracked both. This is possible but thin: Genesis 36:16 reads awkwardly in the Masoretic Text precisely because "duke Korah" is parenthetically inserted into the Eliphaz line, and the Samaritan Pentateuch along with some LXX witnesses drops it. Tov treats this kind of localized disagreement as evidence of a scribal gloss — somebody early in the transmission added Korah to the Eliphaz list to match a different tradition, and the Masoretic Text preserved the gloss. Friedman's source analysis places the Esau toledot as Priestly material that incorporated Edomite king-list traditions from multiple hands, and the duplications are exactly what you'd expect when multiple sources are spliced without full harmonization. The text-critical picture is clearer than the "two Korahs" gambit admits: the contradiction has been visible since antiquity, the manuscripts disagree, and the smoothest reading is that a scribe inserted Korah where he didn't originally belong.
contradictions.scholarship: Emanuel Tov, *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012). Claus Westermann, *Genesis 12-36* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1985). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: Who was Dishon's father?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 36:20-21 and 1 Chronicles 1:38 list Dishon as one of Seir's sons, making Seir the father. A few verses later, Genesis 36:24-25 and 1 Chronicles 1:40-41 say Dishon is Anah's son — and since Anah is Seir's son in 36:20, that makes Dishon Seir's grandson, not son.
contradictions.commentary: This is the same pattern as the Korah contradiction and the apologist response is the same — Keil, Delitzsch, Archer all argue for two different Dishons in the Horite genealogy. The problem is that the Seir genealogy in Genesis 36:20-30 lists only one Dishon (verse 21) and one Dishan, and when it expands the Anah line in verse 25 it names Dishon again without any indication that this is a different person. The repetition with the Aholibamah line ("Anah's daughter Aholibamah") makes the identity explicit — it's the same Anah, therefore the same Dishon. Westermann and Sarna both treat the Horite list as an independent tribal genealogy that the Priestly compiler spliced into the Esau toledot, and the splice produced generational inconsistencies the editor didn't smooth. Friedman's source-critical work on the Esau material shows the same pattern across Genesis 36: two competing systems of organizing the Edomite/Horite clans, combined without harmonization. The "two Dishons" defense requires assuming the genealogist gave identical fathers and sisters to two separate men and never noted it. The critical reading — compiled from incompatible sources — explains the doubling without the acrobatics.
contradictions.scholarship: Claus Westermann, *Genesis 12-36* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1985). Nahum Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary on Gen 36:20-30 (Jewish Publication Society, 1989). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Gary N. Knoppers, *I Chronicles 1-9* (AB; Doubleday, 2003).

contradictions.question: Who brought Joseph into Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 37:28 says the Midianite merchants drew Joseph out of the pit, sold him to the Ishmaelites, and the Ishmaelites brought him to Egypt — a position Genesis 39:1 reinforces. Genesis 37:36, in the very same chapter, says "the Midianites sold him into Egypt." The narrative can't decide which caravan delivered Joseph.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization treats "Midianite" and "Ishmaelite" as overlapping ethnonyms — Judges 8:24 does link the two groups — so Keil, Archer, and Mathews all argue it's one caravan being described two ways. That's not nothing. But Friedman, Baden, and Carr all see this as one of the cleanest fingerprints of source-critical seams in Genesis: the J source has Judah proposing to sell Joseph to Ishmaelites who then carry him to Egypt, while the E source has Reuben wanting to rescue Joseph and Midianite traders pulling him out of the pit unbeknownst to the brothers. The redactor wove them together and produced Genesis 37 as we have it, where Joseph gets "sold" multiple times to different groups in the same paragraph. Speiser's Anchor Bible commentary on Genesis made this case decades ago and the critical consensus has barely moved since. The "overlapping ethnonym" answer doesn't explain why Genesis 37:28 has the Midianites drawing Joseph out and selling him to the Ishmaelites — they're clearly two distinct groups in that verse. Reuben never finds out in the E source, and the brothers' subsequent lie to Jacob makes more sense if they sold Joseph rather than had him stolen. The doublet is the data; the sources are the explanation.
contradictions.scholarship: E. A. Speiser, *Genesis* (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964). Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale, 2012). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). David M. Carr, *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* (Westminster John Knox, 1996). Kenneth A. Mathews, NAC on Gen 37:25-36 (B&H, 2005).

contradictions.question: Where did Joseph's brothers find the missing money?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 42:27 says one brother opened his sack at the lodging place ("the inn") and found the returned money right there. Genesis 43:21 has Judah retelling the story and saying all the brothers found their money at the inn. But Genesis 42:35 shows them emptying their sacks at home in Canaan and being terrified when every bundle of money appears. Money discovery at two different locations.
contradictions.commentary: Keil, Delitzsch, and Archer argue the simplest harmonization: one brother found his money at the inn (42:27), they all got home, emptied the sacks, and discovered the rest (42:35). The retelling in 43:21 collapses the stages. That's plausible on a charitable reading — but it can't be that simple, because Genesis 42:28 has all the brothers reacting with fear to the discovery at the inn ("their heart failed them, and they were afraid"), implying they all knew at the inn. Then they're shown freshly afraid in 42:35 at home, as if discovering it for the first time. Speiser's Anchor commentary and Friedman's source-critical breakdown both treat this as another Joseph-narrative doublet, with J and E each having their own version of the money-discovery scene and the redactor preserving both. In the Yahwist telling, discovery happens at the inn; in the Elohist, discovery happens at home. Stitched together, the brothers seem to discover the same money twice and react to it as a fresh shock each time. The harmonization works only if you accept that the narrative accidentally records the same reaction twice — which is exactly what happens when two sources are combined without full smoothing.
contradictions.scholarship: E. A. Speiser, *Genesis* (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Claus Westermann, *Genesis 37-50* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1986). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: How old was Benjamin when his clan migrated to Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Judah tells Joseph in Genesis 44:20 that Benjamin is "a little one," "a child of his old age" who "cannot leave his father." Two chapters later, Genesis 46:21 lists Benjamin as the father of ten sons among those who went down to Egypt. Infant on one page, patriarch-of-ten on the next.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist solution — Archer, Sailhamer, Mathews — is that "little one" (na'ar / yeled) is used flexibly in Hebrew and Judah is just emphasizing Benjamin's status as the youngest, not his literal age. That works up to a point. Na'ar does have semantic range. But the contradiction isn't only about the word — it's about the whole scene in Genesis 44 being built on Benjamin being young, fragile, and irreplaceable. Judah's entire speech assumes a child who would die away from home. Now do the chronology: Joseph is 17 when sold (Gen 37:2), 30 when he interprets Pharaoh's dream (41:46), and roughly 39 when the family migrates (seven good years plus two famine years). Benjamin is younger but not by much — probably mid-to-late twenties at the migration, already old enough to have fathered the ten sons Genesis 46 attributes to him. The numbers make Judah's "he is but a little one" speech narratively effective but chronologically implausible. Westermann and Speiser both treat the tension as a narrative-source issue: the Joseph novella preserves its own internal chronology emphasizing Benjamin's youth, while the Priestly genealogy in Genesis 46 is working from a different list with ten pre-migration sons. Combining them produces a Benjamin who can't possibly be both.
contradictions.scholarship: Claus Westermann, *Genesis 37-50* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1986). E. A. Speiser, *Genesis* (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964). Kenneth A. Mathews, NAC on Gen 44:18-34 (B&H, 2005). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: Was Mahli the son of Levi?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 8:18 calls Mahli "the son of Levi, the son of Israel" — a direct father-son claim. But every Torah and Chronicles list of Levi's sons (Gen 46:11; Exod 6:16; 1 Chr 6:1, 16; 23:6) names only Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Mahli isn't Levi's son; he's Merari's son (Exod 6:19), making him Levi's grandson.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonizing fix — offered in Keil-Delitzsch and by Archer — is to read "son of Levi" loosely as "descendant of Levi," which Hebrew ben regularly does. Fair. Ben can mean descendant across several generations, and that usage is well-attested. The issue is that Ezra 8:18 isn't just giving a loose tribal affiliation — it's a genealogical chain: "Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel." In that formula, each link is a direct generation elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible. Compare the Levitical genealogies in 1 Chronicles 6, which carefully preserve the three-generation structure Levi → Merari → Mahli. Williamson's commentary on Ezra and Blenkinsopp's both read Ezra 8:18 as a telescoping genealogy in the Chronicler's style — skipping Merari and treating Mahli as representative of the Merarite clan. That's a real scribal convention. But calling it a "convention" doesn't erase that the chain as written is historically incorrect. Telescoping genealogies were a flexible ancient Near Eastern device specifically because writers felt free to compress the record — the existence of the convention is itself evidence that genealogies in the Hebrew Bible shouldn't be taken as literal father-son successions. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the harmonization concedes the critical point while insisting no contradiction exists.
contradictions.scholarship: H. G. M. Williamson, *Ezra, Nehemiah* (WBC 16; Word, 1985). Joseph Blenkinsopp, *Ezra-Nehemiah* (OTL; Westminster John Knox, 1988). Gary N. Knoppers, *I Chronicles 1-9* (AB; Doubleday, 2003). Robert R. Wilson, *Genealogy and History in the Biblical World* (Yale, 1977).

contradictions.question: How many descendants of Jacob and Leah went to Egypt with Jacob?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:9-15a enumerates 32 Leah-descendants by name — Reuben and his four sons, Simeon and his six sons, Levi and his three sons, Judah plus his sons and two grandsons, Issachar and his four sons, Zebulun and his three sons, plus Dinah. That's 32. Genesis 46:15b then totals them at 33.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist answer — Archer's, and you see it in Keil-Delitzsch — is that the count includes Jacob himself, or Leah, or some other extra person the enumerator quietly added. The LXX preserves "thirty-three" and various commentators have juggled whether Dinah counts once or twice, whether Er and Onan (who died in Canaan) belong in the tally, or whether Jacob is implicitly included. Speiser and Westermann both treat the numerical mismatches in Genesis 46 as classic Priestly genealogical arithmetic that doesn't actually add up — the numbers were rounded or symbolic, not computed. The broader pattern confirms this: Genesis 46 totals 70 persons entering Egypt, the Septuagint and Acts 7:14 total 75, and the Masoretic 46:26 gives 66. These numbers all fail to cohere with each other in any arithmetic sense. Friedman treats the 70-count as schematic — it matches the 70 nations of Genesis 10 — rather than literal. The off-by-one in Genesis 46:15 is a small instance of a larger pattern: Priestly genealogies are built for theological symmetry, not arithmetic accuracy. The harmonizations that rescue each individual discrepancy end up conceding that the text wasn't trying to pass a counting test in the first place.
contradictions.scholarship: E. A. Speiser, *Genesis* (AB 1; Doubleday, 1964). Claus Westermann, *Genesis 37-50* (Continental Commentary; Fortress, 1986). Richard Elliott Friedman, *Commentary on the Torah* (HarperOne, 2001). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: Will God destroy those that intermarry?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 7:3-4 bans intermarriage with the Canaanite nations on pain of God's anger destroying the offender "suddenly." Genesis 46:20 records Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potipherah, priest of the Egyptian sun-god at On/Heliopolis — a foreign priestess-daughter — with no divine pushback. The law says destruction; the narrative shows endorsement.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist move, run by Kaiser and Archer, is that Deuteronomy 7 targets specifically the seven Canaanite nations and their idolatry, not all foreign unions, and that Joseph's Egyptian marriage falls outside that list. Narrow the category, shrink the problem. That works partially — Deuteronomy 7:1 does name specific peoples. But Ezra 9-10 and Nehemiah 13 extend the prohibition much wider, treating any marriage to non-Israelites as a defilement, and they explicitly appeal to the Deuteronomic law as their warrant. So by the post-exilic period, the principle had clearly generalized. Christine Hayes and Shaye Cohen have both mapped how intermarriage theology hardened from the monarchic period through the Second Temple era — the J and E sources are comfortable with Joseph marrying an Egyptian priest's daughter, Moses marrying Zipporah the Midianite, Boaz marrying Ruth the Moabite (who is specifically one of the prohibited nations under Deut 23:3), while Deuteronomic and Priestly writers get increasingly anxious about foreign wives. The contradiction isn't within a single author's work; it's between different theological generations that produced incompatible ethics and then got bound together. Joseph's marriage stands in the text as a patriarchal-era artifact that the later Deuteronomic editors never scrubbed.
contradictions.scholarship: Christine E. Hayes, *Gentile Impurities and Jewish Identities* (Oxford, 2002). Shaye J. D. Cohen, *The Beginnings of Jewishness* (University of California, 1999). Joseph Blenkinsopp, *Ezra-Nehemiah* (OTL; Westminster John Knox, 1988). Walter C. Kaiser, *Hard Sayings of the Bible* (IVP, 1996).

contradictions.question: Were Naaman and Ard the sons or the grandsons of Benjamin?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:21 lists Naaman and Ard as sons of Benjamin who migrated to Egypt. Numbers 26:40 lists Ard and Naaman as sons of Bela — making them Benjamin's grandsons, not his sons. Same names, different generational slots.
contradictions.commentary: The go-to apologist solution is telescoping: Archer and Kaiser both argue that Genesis 46:21 lumps descendants without strict generational markers and that Numbers 26 gives the more precise family tree. Possible, but it runs into the same problem we saw with Benjamin's age — if Benjamin was young enough in Genesis 44 to be called a "little one," the presence of ten sons and multiple grandsons at the migration becomes chronologically impossible. Friedman, Baden, and Carr place Genesis 46:8-27 in the Priestly tribal-list tradition and note that the Priestly census lists in Numbers are working from overlapping but not identical genealogical data. The Samaritan Pentateuch and LXX preserve variant readings in both passages that smooth some of the tension — another indication that ancient copyists were already trying to reconcile the lists and failing. Knoppers' work on Chronicles shows that the Chronicler's parallel list in 1 Chronicles 7:6-12 doesn't match either Genesis or Numbers cleanly, giving three distinct Benjaminite genealogies that disagree on generation counts and names. Three independent list-traditions, three incompatible family trees. The "telescoping" answer papers over a real data problem: the tribal censuses don't agree with each other, full stop.
contradictions.scholarship: Gary N. Knoppers, *I Chronicles 1-9* (AB; Doubleday, 2003). Joel S. Baden, *The Composition of the Pentateuch* (Yale, 2012). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Gleason Archer, *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (Zondervan, 1982).

contradictions.question: How many were in Jacob's family when they came into Egypt?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 46:27, Exodus 1:5, and Deuteronomy 10:22 all put the migration number at 70. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:14 puts it at 75. Two counts, five people apart.
contradictions.commentary: This one has a textual solution that apologists and critics actually agree on at the front end — the 75-count comes from the Septuagint, which adds five of Joseph's Egyptian-born grandsons to the tally in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5. The Dead Sea Scrolls fragments 4QGen-Exod-a and 4QExod-b both agree with the LXX reading of 75. So Luke (writing Acts) was working from the Greek Old Testament, which is why his Stephen speech says 75 while the Masoretic-based English translations say 70. That's the textual fix, and it's real. But notice what the harmonization concedes: the New Testament author is quoting a version of the Hebrew Bible that differs from the version Christians and Jews eventually canonized, and the two versions don't agree on basic numerical facts. Emanuel Tov's work on the Pentateuch textual history shows that the 70/75 discrepancy is part of a broader pattern where the LXX, MT, and Samaritan Pentateuch preserve three different editorial layers of Genesis-Exodus, each with its own numbers. Calling this "not a contradiction" requires you to pick which Hebrew Bible is the real one and ignore that the New Testament author picked a different one. The text of Acts is internally consistent with the text Luke had. The contradiction is between Luke's Bible and the Bible most of his later readers inherited. That is of course a text-critical observation, not a doctrinal one.
contradictions.scholarship: Emanuel Tov, *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012). Eugene Ulrich, *The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Developmental Composition of the Bible* (Brill, 2015). C. K. Barrett, *Acts of the Apostles* (ICC; T&T Clark, 1994). Richard I. Pervo, *Acts* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 2009).

contradictions.question: What were the twelve tribes of Israel (Jacob)?
contradictions.summary: The Hebrew Bible and New Testament preserve six different lists of the "twelve tribes" of Israel — Gen 49, Num 1, Num 13, Deut 33, Ezek 48, Rev 7 — and no two lists match. Across the six, fourteen different tribal names appear. Only eight tribes appear on every list. Simeon, Levi, Dan, Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh each get dropped somewhere.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist explanation — Archer, Wenham, LaSor — is that the "twelve tribes" is a flexible theological schema rather than a strict roster. Levi gets counted or not depending on whether you're listing land-allotment tribes or worship-officiant tribes; Joseph gets split into Ephraim and Manasseh when you need to replace Levi; the number twelve is preserved even when the individual names shift. That's accurate as description. The problem is what this concedes: the "twelve tribes" is a theological scaffold, not a historical memory. Mark Smith and Daniel Fleming both argue that Israel's tribal structure was fluid, politically contingent, and differently remembered by different sources at different times — Ephraim dominates northern lists, Judah dominates southern lists, the Levitical priesthood had its own interests in how tribes got counted. The Revelation 7 list drops Dan and Ephraim, which makes sense if you're a late first-century Christian writer working from a tradition that associated those tribes with apostasy (a trope visible in rabbinic literature). Ezekiel 48 reorganizes tribal land allotments around a future-ideal geography rather than historical facts. The number twelve is preserved across all six lists precisely because twelve is the theologically loaded number — three tribes per compass point around the tabernacle, twelve apostles, twelve foundation stones in the New Jerusalem. When the names change but the total doesn't, the scaffold is doing the work, not the memory. A historical twelve-tribe confederation may have existed in Israel's past, but the biblical lists are theological projections, not archives.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, *The Memoirs of God* (Fortress, 2004). Daniel E. Fleming, *The Legacy of Israel in Judah's Bible* (Cambridge, 2012). Zecharia Kallai, *Historical Geography of the Bible: The Tribal Territories of Israel* (Brill, 1986). David Noel Freedman, *Pottery, Poetry, and Prophecy* (Eisenbrauns, 1980).

contradictions.question: Where was Jacob buried?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 50:13 has Jacob's sons carrying him into Canaan and burying him in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, the family tomb purchased by Abraham. Stephen in Acts 7:15-16 says Jacob was "carried over into Shechem, and laid in the sepulchre that Abraham bought" — which is fifty miles north of Machpelah, and which Abraham never bought. The speech in Acts gets both the location and the buyer wrong.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist strategy — Bruce, Marshall, Archer, Bock — is that Stephen is telescoping two different burials: Jacob at Machpelah and Joseph and his brothers at Shechem (Joshua 24:32 has Joseph's bones reburied there). The speech conflates the two for rhetorical compression, and the "Abraham bought" reference is a slip for Jacob's purchase of the Shechem plot in Genesis 33:19. That's one way to read it. But even with the most generous telescoping, Acts 7:16 explicitly says Jacob and the fathers were buried in Shechem and that Abraham bought the tomb. Genesis is unambiguous on both points — Jacob was not buried at Shechem and Abraham did not buy the Shechem plot. Pervo's Hermeneia commentary on Acts treats this as a historical error in the Lucan source rather than a compression technique, and Fitzmyer's Anchor commentary at least concedes the tension without resolving it. The deeper issue: Stephen's speech has multiple demonstrable factual errors against the Hebrew Bible (Abraham's departure timing, the 400 vs. 430 years, the Shechem burial) and the pattern suggests Luke is drawing on a tradition whose details don't line up with canonical Genesis. Either Stephen is wrong, Luke is wrong, or the speech is reflecting a non-canonical Samaritan-influenced tradition that located the patriarchal tombs at Shechem. Take your pick — none of those options rescue inerrancy.
contradictions.scholarship: Richard I. Pervo, *Acts* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 2009). Joseph A. Fitzmyer, *The Acts of the Apostles* (AB 31; Doubleday, 1998). C. K. Barrett, *Acts of the Apostles* (ICC; T&T Clark, 1994). Darrell L. Bock, *Acts* (BECNT; Baker, 2007).

contradictions.question: Is it wrong to lie?
contradictions.summary: The Decalogue and a long chorus of prophetic, wisdom, and epistolary texts prohibit lying absolutely — false witness, false reports, deception are abominations. Revelation 21:8 and 21:27 even send liars to the lake of fire. But Exodus 1:18-20 has the Hebrew midwives lying to Pharaoh about why they didn't kill the newborn boys, and God explicitly "deals well" with them for it. Lying merits hellfire in one place and divine reward in another.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist scaffolding — Kaiser, Geisler, Copan — is "graded absolutism": moral commands form a hierarchy, and when commands conflict (don't lie vs. don't let babies die), obeying the higher one absolves you for violating the lower one. Fine as ethical theory. But watch what happens to the text. Exodus 1:20 doesn't say "God understood they had to lie" or "God forgave them for lying" — it says God blessed them and gave them households because of it. The Rahab case in Joshua 2 runs the same pattern: she lies to the Jericho authorities about the spies and is rewarded with survival, property, and ancestry in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5). James 2:25 explicitly praises Rahab's deception as righteous works. Meanwhile, Proverbs and Revelation treat lying as categorically disqualifying. Dale Allison's work on ethics in early Judaism and Christianity shows this tension wasn't resolved within the biblical corpus — different writers operated with different ethical grammars. The Holiness Code and prophetic tradition were absolutist; the narrative traditions were consequentialist when it suited them. The graded-absolutism defense works as a philosophical overlay but requires admitting that the Bible itself doesn't articulate the hierarchy. That framework was imposed later to reconcile texts that were already in conflict.
contradictions.scholarship: Dale C. Allison, *The Sermon on the Mount: Inspiring the Moral Imagination* (Herder, 1999). John J. Collins, *Introduction to the Hebrew Bible*, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2018). Norman L. Geisler, *Christian Ethics*, 2nd ed. (Baker Academic, 2010). Paul Copan, *Is God a Moral Monster?* (Baker, 2011).

contradictions.question: Did Moses fear the king?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 2:14-15 says Moses feared when he learned his killing of the Egyptian was known, and he fled from Pharaoh's face. Hebrews 11:27 retells the same departure: "By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king." The Torah says he feared and fled; Hebrews says he didn't fear at all.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist workaround, pressed by Lane, Cockerill, and Bruce, is that Hebrews 11:27 isn't describing Moses' flight to Midian in Exodus 2 but rather the later Exodus-from-Egypt event when Moses led the people out — which puts a different framing on the "faith" and "not fearing" language. That reading has real merit: Hebrews 11:28 immediately describes the Passover, so the sequence favors the Exodus departure over the Midian flight. Problem: Hebrews 11:27 says "he forsook Egypt" in the singular, Moses-as-individual sense, and in the plain narrative order of Exodus 2, Moses' individual flight is exactly what's being described. Attridge's Hermeneia commentary lays out the ambiguity and concedes that the author of Hebrews is working from a typologically reworked memory of Moses rather than a strict reading of Exodus. Koester's Anchor Yale commentary on Hebrews treats the verse as a theological gloss on Moses' character that smooths over Exodus 2's "fear" language in service of the faith-catalog structure of Hebrews 11. Either Hebrews is referring to the Exodus (which wasn't "by faith" alone — it was after a year of plagues and divine coercion) or it's referring to Moses' Midian flight (which Exodus explicitly says was motivated by fear). Either reading generates a conflict with some piece of the Torah narrative. Take your pick.
contradictions.scholarship: Harold W. Attridge, *Hebrews* (Hermeneia; Fortress, 1989). Craig R. Koester, *Hebrews* (AB 36; Doubleday, 2001). William L. Lane, *Hebrews 9-13* (WBC 47B; Word, 1991). Gareth L. Cockerill, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (NICNT; Eerdmans, 2012).

contradictions.question: Who appeared to Moses in the burning bush?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 3:2 says "the angel of the LORD" appeared to Moses in the flame, and Acts 7:35 confirms it was an angel. But Exodus 3:4 in the same passage shifts and says "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush," and Mark 12:26 has Jesus himself affirm that God spoke to Moses at the bush. Same encounter, two different speakers.
contradictions.commentary: The traditional solution — endorsed by Calvin, carried by Kaiser, Walton, and Stuart — is that "the angel of Yahweh" is a functional stand-in for Yahweh himself throughout the Hebrew Bible, so "angel" and "God" can name the same being without contradiction. Some apologists go further and read the angel as a pre-incarnate Christophany. The pre-incarnate-Christ reading is a dogmatic overlay, not anything the text suggests. But even the broader "angel as God-surrogate" claim is doing heavy lifting. Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have mapped the mal'akh YHWH formula across Hebrew Bible texts and shown it functions inconsistently — sometimes as Yahweh himself in disguise (Gen 16, Gen 22), sometimes as a genuinely separate emissary (Num 22, 2 Sam 24). In Exodus 3 the narrative oscillates: verse 2 has the angel appearing in the flame, verse 4 has Yahweh and Elohim both speaking. Friedman's source analysis splits the passage between J and E, each using different terms for the divine speaker. Carr, Baden, and Propp all treat the angel/God alternation in Exodus 3 as a redactor's seam rather than a unified theology — the E source tends to use "angel" or "God" circumlocutions while J uses "Yahweh" directly. The harmonization works at the level of mature second-temple theology (where "angel of Yahweh" got systematized as an avatar doctrine), but the Exodus 3 text itself preserves two source-strands with different names for who showed up at the bush.
contradictions.scholarship: Mark S. Smith, *The Early History of God* (Eerdmans, 2002). Benjamin D. Sommer, *The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel* (Cambridge, 2009). William H. C. Propp, *Exodus 1-18* (AB 2; Doubleday, 1999). Richard Elliott Friedman, *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (HarperOne, 2003). Douglas K. Stuart, NAC on Exod 3:1-6 (B&H, 2006).
